Q: How to retrieve argv and argc in assembly language for x86_64 processors on Linux (SYSTEM V) OS A:

The argc/argv are pushed by OS on stack, so your assembly code needs to pop them out from stack into registers in order to use them. There's a tutorial about it with detailed diagram of stack layout as well as demo code to show the command line arguments using just assembly code. See the document/tutorial from this GitHub repo:

https://github.com/LilSuperUser/x86_64-asm-tutorials/blob/main/notes/013-CLI_arguments.md

Note that the example assembly code shown in the tutorial is in "nasm" format. In order to use it, you will need to install "nasm". On Debian distro (or all those derived from Debian), you can install it with this commans:

sudo apt install nasm

To generate the executable:

nasm -f elf64 sample.s -o sample.o
ld sample.o -o sample

For other distros, the install command would be different but you probably knew how already.

Q: How to find all image tags of a running Docker container? A:

Getting all the tags for a particular image (e.g. image backing a running container) can surely be done with Skopeo, but it's often not the fastest way to do it.

Whether you can get an answer quicker depends on the registry. Some registries have special endpoints that avoid expensive scans; others have unique APIs (e.g., GitHub Packages API) that can help. For a tool that tries to use the optimal method for each registry, you can try my https://github.com/huyz/container-image-tags

Q: How to plot specific data types in matplotlib A:

In addition to others' answers, you can also use seaborn.relplot:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, parse_dates=["Date_Hour"], date_format="%m/%d/%y %H:%M")
sns.relplot(
    df,
    x="Date_Hour",
    y="N2O_flux",
    row="Genotype",
    col="Fertilizer",
    hue="Replicate",
    kind="line",  # or "scatter" if you prefer
    marker="o",
)
plt.show()

Q: If I drop & then recreate table with the same name, do associated objects (stored procedures, views, triggers) handle that? A:

YES, you do need to refresh the views and procedures in many cases.

There are cases when the referencing code is invalidated. For example, if you change the order columns, and the code uses SELECT *, the order of those output columns will change. Any added columns will not be shown, and if you remove a column then a binding error will occur.

See for example this fiddle.

There may be other cases when changes are made to the table. I'm not sure which changes, but for example if you add Row Level Security, Temporal Table etc then you may get issues.

The simplest solution is to just run sp_refreshsqlmodule on all referencing modules just to be safe. You can find all those modules using sys.dm_sql_referencing_entities

Q: Maven clean fails with AccessDeniedException while compile succeeds on Windows 11 A:

My advice is

  1. Test the workaround:

2.      .\mvnw.cmd clean -Dmaven.clean.force=true

  1. If that succeeds, test Clean Plugin 3.4.1.

  2. If 3.4.1 succeeds reliably, keep 3.4.1 for now rather than fighting Windows deletion behavior.

  3. If you want to investigate further, use Microsoft's Sysinternals Process Explorer/Handle to determine whether something has an open filesystem handle. Maven's own FAQ recommends these tools for Windows deletion failures. A

So, no, I don't see anything wrong with your project configuration from what you've shown. The combination of Windows + maven-clean-plugin:3.5.0 + an AccessDeniedException while deleting an otherwise ordinary target\classes package directory is a known pattern, and your successful manual deletion makes a genuine permissions problem particularly unlikely.

Q: how to commit change while leaving all the staged and unstaged changes? A:

The way to do it is to bypass standard high-level commands and write the fix directly using low-level Git plumbing commands.

This avoids merge conflicts because you modify the initial commit object directly in the background.

Create an isolated commit with the target fix:

git commit-tree $(git write-tree) -m "bug line changed"

This outputs a brand new commit hash in your terminal. Copy that hash, which we will call FIX_COMMIT_HASH.

Assuming this is your very first commit on the master/main branch:

git update-ref refs/heads/main FIX_COMMIT_HASH

If you are working deeper in a branch history rather than the initial commit, replace refs/heads/main with your specific branch name or target commit reference.
